story:
The gym smelled like popcorn and floor wax, and Felix had his phone out before the buzzer even started the game. His best friend Dara leaned over from the next bleacher.

"You're checking baseball stats at a basketball game?"

"It matters," Felix said. "My dad says Justice was better than Jeter in the nineties. My uncle says Jeter. I'm settling it." He tapped through the seasons, one by one, and felt his stomach drop a little. In 1995, David Justice had the higher batting average. In 1996, David Justice had the higher batting average again. He scrolled back up to check, then down again, calibrating his eyes to the columns the way he'd line up a free throw. Same result both years.

"Justice," he announced. "Twice. Case closed."

Dara snatched the phone. "Then add them together. Two seasons, one winner." She found the combined numbers and went quiet. Then she turned the screen toward him, and Felix read it twice, but the numbers did not change their minds. Jeter's two-year average was higher.

"That's broken," Felix said. "He lost both years. How does he win the whole thing?" Down on the court, the home team was committing foul after foul, and the crowd groaned with each whistle. Felix barely heard it. He tried adding the averages himself, then multiplying, then starting over, and nothing came out the way the screen said. He passed the phone along the row to his older sister, Priya, who was home from college and only came to games when she wanted the nachos.

"Look at this," he said. "Justice beats Jeter in ninety-five, Justice beats Jeter in ninety-six, and then combined, Jeter's on top."

Priya squinted at it, shrugged, and handed it back. "Numbers are weird," she said, and went back to the nachos. That was the cost of asking Priya anything.

The buzzer sounded for halftime with the home team down by twelve. Felix kept scrolling while the cheerleaders tumbled across the floor. The whole game was numbers too, he realized. Field goal percentage, rankings, that "significant scoring drought" the announcer kept mentioning, as if four empty minutes could be squeezed into one tidy phrase. All those shots, all those misses, pressed into a single figure, like a cliff slowly worn down to one smooth number. Erosion, his science teacher would call it.

The twist came in the fourth quarter, when Dara nudged him, grinning, holding the phone. "I found it. It's a famous thing. Justice, Jeter, all of it."

"Does it say why?"

"Doesn't matter," Dara said. "Your dad and your uncle were both right."

The home team lost by two on a last-second shot that rimmed out. On the walk to the parking lot, Felix texted his dad one line: "Everybody won." The reply came back before he reached the car: "That's not an answer."

story:
Charlotte slid into her chair just as her mother set down the pasta bowl with a clunk. Her mother had been on the phone all afternoon with the corporation's office in another city, and now she was stirring parmesan into the pot like it had personally offended her.

"You okay, Mom?" Charlotte's little brother Theo asked with his mouth full. He had been building an intricate fortress out of breadstick sticks, and their mother's mood was clearly messing with his architecture plans.

"I'm fine," their mother said, in the voice that meant the opposite. "The merger means half our team might migrate to the Chicago office next spring. I found out an hour ago. My anxiety has been through the roof since."

Charlotte watched her mother's hands, noticed the way she kept checking her phone even though it was silent. She remembered what Zoe had told her at lunch, after Zoe had failed her math quiz. "My counselor says coping means the ways you handle stress or hard feelings," Zoe had said, counting on her fingers. "Healthy coping is stuff like exercise, getting enough sleep, and talking with someone you trust. I used to just stay up scrolling, which is the bad kind." Charlotte had rolled her eyes at the time. Now she wondered.

She decided to test it. "Mom, remember when you made us walk the loop at the park after Grandpa's funeral, and you said moving helps you think?" she asked. "Want to go after dinner? Theo can come."

"I have emails," her mother said.

"Zoe says talking to someone you trust counts as coping too," Charlotte said. "So we could walk and you could talk. That's two healthy ones at once."

Theo looked up from his fortress, which had collapsed during the phone-checking. "I want to come. I'll rebuild the walls outside with sticks."

Their father raised his eyebrows at their mother. "The emails will still be there at nine," he said.

They walked the loop while the sky went orange. Theo collected sticks for a new fortress and their mother talked, haltingly at first, about boundaries she should have set months ago, about saying no to the extra projects that had swallowed her whole spring. By the second lap her shoulders had dropped an inch, though Charlotte noticed she still checked her phone twice at the corner where the signal came back.

At bedtime, Charlotte found her mother on the porch with her laptop, working anyway, because the merger was still happening and a walk could not change that. But she had also left her office chair pushed back from the desk, pointed toward the door, and a sticky note stuck to the screen that said "9:00, park?" Tomorrow the anxiety would be back, Charlotte knew. Still, she texted Zoe: "It worked on my mom. Mostly." Zoe sent back a running emoji and the words "sleep counts too." Charlotte put her phone in the drawer, where it buzzed once, twice, and then went quiet.

Rosalie spread her supplies across the picnic table: a stack of square paper, a magnifying lens she used for examining folds, and a bottle of water that was already going warm in the afternoon sun. The library origami club was meeting on Saturday, and she had promised to bring a paper crane that actually stood up. Three cranes lay in the grass, each one slumping over like it had given up.

Her neighbor Marcus climbed over the fence, the way he always did, and picked up one of the failed birds. "Still the same problem," he said, turning it toward the light. "The neck folds are too loose."

"I know that," Rosalie said. "What I don't know is why they keep coming out loose when I do exactly what the diagram says." She flattened the third crane and studied the creases through her lens. Each fold looked sharp on top, but when she held the paper up, she could see faint ghost lines underneath, running the wrong direction. Those hidden creases had been pressed into the paper during her earlier failed attempts. The problem was not in the fold she was making now; it was in the folds she had made before.

She tried to paraphrase the idea for Marcus. "So it's like the paper remembers." He shrugged, so she grabbed a fresh square. "Watch. No practice creases, no reusing paper." She folded slowly, and this time the crane's neck stood stiff and straight, its head pointing at the sky.

Marcus sat down on the bench. "Hey, at the club meeting, Priya said the word origami means something different. She claims it just means folding."

"It's both parts," Rosalie said. "Origami comes from 'ori', meaning to fold, and 'kami', meaning paper."

Marcus frowned. "Then Priya's only got half of it."

"You can tell her Saturday," Rosalie said. "Bring a crane so she knows you actually fold." He borrowed a square of paper and tried to copy her steps, but his bird turned out crooked, and after a minute of pressing and pressing at the wing he gave up and dropped it in the grass.

"That was a vain effort," he admitted, and Rosalie laughed. She lined up her one good crane on the table where the sun caught it, and set a fresh square beside it for tomorrow.

activity: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
story:
The minivan smelled like sunscreen and French fries, and Ariana was pretending not to sniff her own gym shirt when her little brother, Milo, leaned over from the back seat. "You smell like the boys' locker room," he announced, delighted with himself.

"Rude," Ariana said, but she cranked the window down anyway. She had showered after gym. She had even put on the deodorant she'd bought last month, the one with the intricate swirl design on the stick that had fooled her into thinking it was fancy. So why could she still smell herself? She turned the question over while Mom navigated traffic toward Grandma's house.

Then she remembered Thanksgiving, when her cousin Dez had been home from college. Some kid at the adult table had asked why his deodorant suddenly mattered, and Dez had laughed and said, "Fresh sweat has almost no smell. Body odor comes when bacteria on your skin break down sweat from the armpit glands, and those glands don't kick in until puberty." Ariana had been half listening then, busy with pie. Now the words snapped into place like a puzzle she'd finally found the edge of. That was why she'd never needed deodorant before this year. It wasn't that she'd gotten lazy. Her whole armpit situation had been rewritten.

She had a hypothesis, and a hypothesis needed a test. "Milo," she said, spinning around in her seatbelt, "smell my wrist." Mom said, "Eyes forward, please," but Milo was already grabbing her arm and taking a huge sniff. "Nothing," he reported. "Soap, I guess." "Exactly!" Ariana said. "My wrists sweat, but no smell. So it's not sweat itself." She was so excited she nearly bounced off the seat. "It's the armpit glands. Puberty ones. Bacteria eat their sweat and that's the smell. I'm basically running an experiment right now."

"You're basically being weird," Milo said, but he was grinning, already sniffing his own wrist like a detective. Mom muttered something about science happening in the car instead of at the dinner table, and Ariana pulled out her phone to text Dez: "Your armpit speech just solved my whole afternoon." She paused before sending, already anticipating the next problem. If bacteria were the culprit, was her deodorant even the right kind? Maybe she needed the antibacterial one, the one with the ingredient list long as a polymer chain, which was the only thing she'd retained from science class this week. "Next stop, the drugstore," she said to the windshield. Mom sighed. "We're going to Grandma's." "Then after Grandma's. This is important, Mom. This is a matter of reputation." Milo snickered. "Reputation of what, Stinky?" Ariana flicked his cap sideways and grinned at the road ahead.

story:
Easton lay on his bed with three crumpled tissues on the blanket and his tablet propped against a pillow. His cold was almost gone, but his mother had made him stay home one more day, and he had spent most of that day wondering about one thing. Two weeks ago his sister Priya had a cold, and he had caught it from her. Last winter he had caught a different one from his friend Marcus. His flu shot had protected him against the flu every year, so why was there no shot like that for colds?

He typed his question into the search bar. The first answer made him sit up straight against the pillows. More than 200 different viruses could cause the common cold. He read the number twice, then said it out loud to the empty room. Two hundred. And the page said rhinoviruses are the most frequent cause, which meant some little family of viruses he had never heard of was responsible for more of his sniffles than anything else.

Priya appeared in the doorway holding two mugs of tea. "Mom said to bring you this. Why do you look like you solved a mystery?"

"Because I kind of did," Easton said. "I always blamed you for my colds. But you can't make a vaccine that covers two hundred different viruses the way the flu shot covers the flu. That's why nobody's ever given us one." He turned the tablet toward her. "Rhinoviruses. That's what usually gets us."

Priya set the mugs down and climbed onto the end of his bed. "Okay, but here's my problem. I want to stop catching your colds, since you clearly can't stop catching mine." She pulled a marker from her pocket, the special gold one she had been saving for a school poster, and drew a line down the middle of a tissue. "Sick side and healthy side."

Easton tested her idea against what he had just read. "That works for us, but it doesn't work for the world," he said. "We could hide from each other forever and still get colds, because there are so many different viruses out there. Any one of them could be the one that gets you next." Priya frowned at her golden line, clearly wanting a better answer than that.

"Then we do both," she decided. "Tissue rule in this house, and you wash your hands before you touch my mug." She traded him her tea for the tablet and started reading, and after a minute she looked up with an exceptional grin, the kind she saved for good ideas. "I'm going to tell my class this on Monday. Two hundred viruses, and rhinoviruses win. I'll sound like a health diplomat negotiating peace between us."

"Just don't cough on my poster markers," Easton said, and she threw a clean tissue at him, and it landed right on the sick side of the line.

story:
Jaxson sat cross-legged on Devin's bedroom floor with his phone balanced on one knee, watching the group chat scroll. Devin's little sister thumped down the hallway outside, and somewhere below them the kitchen TV murmured through the floor. The chat was for planning Saturday at the skate park, but nobody had answered Jaxson's last three messages. He had written "anyone going early?" an hour ago, and it sat there like a coin dropped in an empty well.

Then Marcus posted, "I can come at ten." Right after, Priya posted, "me too, bringing my new board." Jaxson's question had never existed to them. He stared at his screen and thought about it. It wasn't that they disliked him. It was something quieter, something about how a small gray bubble among thirty others just vanished. He needed his message to have weight without being annoying, and he wasn't sure those were even different things yet.

He typed "WHERE ARE YOU GUYS MEETING" and hit send before he could second-guess himself. For three seconds nothing happened. Then Priya replied, "why are you yelling?" Marcus sent a single wide-eyed emoji. Jaxson's ears went hot. Yelling? He hadn't shouted a word out loud. But sitting there on Devin's floor, hearing how loud those capital letters looked against Priya's calm lowercase reply, he could see what she meant. In here, on the screen, caps were a raised voice, even in a silent room.

"It's like you walked into a library and hollered," Devin said, peering over from his bed. Jaxson had to digest that for a moment. The same words could be quiet or loud depending only on their shape. It was a small paradox: he had used the biggest letters to be noticed, and the bigness itself was what made him look wrong. "Sorry," he typed, all lowercase. "ten works for me too. I'll bring the extra bearings."

"finally someone has bearings," Priya answered, and Marcus sent a row of thumbs-up. Jaxson noticed the pattern then. Priya used lowercase even when she was excited. Marcus never used periods unless he was serious. The chat had rules nobody had posted, and he had been reading them wrong this whole time, like standing too close to people without knowing it.

He put the phone face-down on the carpet and listened to the TV muttering below, Devin's sister's footsteps, the radiator ticking. The morning was still going to be awkward maybe. But it was a solvable kind of awkward. He picked the phone back up and typed slowly, in ordinary small letters, "want me to come early and help set the ramp?" Priya's reply came fast: "yes please." Jaxson grinned at the screen and said, "Marcus owes me a soda for the bearings."

story:
The community center gym smelled like floor wax and old popcorn, and Victor liked it best on Tuesdays, when the whole basketball season still stretched out ahead of him. This Tuesday, though, Coach Reyes had something different planned. She dragged a thick rope out of the equipment closet and told them to try tug-of-war before shooting drills, just for fun, just to see. Victor was picked for the six-person side, and even though their team weighed more than the five-person side, they lost. Twice.

"That's strange," Coach Reyes said, coiling the rope. "You all look like you're easing off out there." She didn't say it in a mean way, but Victor felt his ears go hot, because it was true. When he pulled with five others, he couldn't tell if he was pulling hard or hardly at all.

That night he typed tug of war pulling less with more people into the library computer, mostly to prove it wasn't his imagination. He found it right away. "In 1913 Max Ringelmann reported that as more people pulled on a rope together, each person's average pull became smaller," he read. So a bigger team didn't automatically pull harder. Each person's average pull shrank. He wrote it on a scrap of paper and folded it into his sock drawer, then thought better of it and put it in his gym bag instead. The tournament was Saturday, and Coach Reyes had announced that tug-of-war would open it, one pull against the Riverside team to start the day.

At Thursday practice, Victor asked to try something. "Let's pull one at a time," he said. "Watch the rope move each time, so everybody knows what their own pull looks like." Marisol went first, and the rope jerked a clear arm's length. Then Devon, then Victor, each one marked with a sneaker on the floor. After that, when all six pulled together, Victor counted under his breath, one two pull, one two pull, and the rope moved farther than it had on Tuesday.

"It's like the whole center," Marisol said, wiping her hands on her shorts. "My mom calls it an ecosystem. Basketball, the garden club, us. Everything works when everybody does their part." Devon, who had spent Tuesday sulking that the rope game was pointless and that they'd lost because of Marisol, nudged her shoulder. "Okay, I take it back. You were pulling fine. I just couldn't see it."

Saturday morning came gray and cool, and the permanent trophy case gleamed by the front doors, waiting for a new plaque with the winner's name. Riverside's team was bigger, eight to their six, and their captain grinned like the win was already his. The whistle blew. Victor gripped the rough rope, found the rhythm in his head, and heard five teammates breathing in time beside him. The red flag in the rope's center slid, steady as anything, across the painted line.

story:
Hazel stood in her grandmother's crowded living room holding a wrapped box of almond cookies and trying to remember the plan. Her French cousins were arriving any minute, and her grandmother had said the meal would be on the table at six o'clock sharp, which gave Hazel exactly one hour to figure out the kissing thing before she embarrassed herself in front of everyone.

The trouble had started at the airport that morning. Aunt Céline had swept in and kissed Hazel's cheeks twice, left then right, while Uncle Marc had given her three kisses, which meant Hazel had to tilt her head an extra time and nearly bonbed noses with him. Then Coco, who was thirteen like Hazel, had kissed her twice again. Hazel smiled through all of it, but inside she was thinking hard. Her aunt and uncle were from the same family, so why didn't they match?

The doorbell rang, and the room turned turbulent with relatives hugging, untying scarves, and passing gifts. Coco's little brother Théo came in shaking rain off his jacket like a dog, and their grandmother handed out presents, insisting that the smallest children open theirs first, which was different from Hazel's house, where everyone waited and tore in at once. Hazel put her cookies on the gift table, then edged toward Coco in the kitchen, where a pot of mussels was steaming and someone was pulling the black hulls off bread slices that had gone soggy in the rain.

"Can I ask you something?" Hazel said. "At the airport, your mom kissed me two times, but your uncle did three. Did I do it wrong?"

Coco laughed, not meanly. "You did fine. It's called la bise," she said. "The number of kisses depends on where you live in France. My mom's from a place where it's two. Uncle Marc grew up somewhere it's three."

Hazel felt like a code had cracked open. It wasn't about her, or about being polite or rude; it was a pattern, like area codes. She wanted to test it. When Grand-mère Lucie arrived early, before the others, Hazel watched carefully. Two kisses. "You're from the same region as Aunt Céline," Hazel said, and Grand-mère Lucie beamed and kissed her twice more, right there on the spot.

By the time everyone sat down at six, with elbows off the table because in this house hands rested beside the plate, Hazel had counted kisses from four more relatives and gotten every single one right. Uncle Marc leaned over during the salad course and said, "You have conquered the bise, Hazel. Better than my own son." Théo, mid-mussels, protested loudly, and the whole table dissolved into laughter while Hazel ducked her head, grinning, and passed the bread.

The highway signs said sixty more miles to the coast, and Luca's little brother Nico had already asked "are we there yet" four times, which had to be some kind of record. Their dad drummed the steering wheel. Their mom read the map out loud even though the GPS was talking too, because she didn't trust it. She said it was biased toward highways.

Luca watched the pine trees flick past the window and thought about last summer, the same beach, the same cramped car. That was the trip when he'd made his big mistake. He'd been in the water when he felt the ocean start to pull, a steady tug out toward the deep, and he'd rebelled against it, swimming straight back toward the sand with everything he had. The harder he fought, the farther out he went, until his arms burned and his dad had to splash in and drag him back. The lifeguard on duty had scolded him gently afterward, and Luca had nodded without really listening, too embarrassed.

"What's that sign say again?" Nico asked now, digging through the photos on Mom's phone. He'd found one from the beach boardwalk, a yellow warning sign with a picture of a swimmer and an arrow.

"Rip current," Luca said. "It's the thing that got me last year."

"What do you do if the water pulls you out? Like, for real?"

Luca was quiet for a second. He'd thought about it all winter, replaying that afternoon, wondering what he should have done instead of panicking. He'd even tested an idea in the pool at school, swimming along the lane line sideways instead of turning against the current the teacher made with the paddle. It was slower, and it felt wrong, like giving up, but it worked. "You don't swim straight back at the beach," he said. "That's what I did, and it just kept pulling. You swim parallel to the beach instead, along the shoreline. The current's narrow, so you get out of it that way, and then you can come in."

"You're sure? You tried it?"

"Sort of. And the lifeguard said the same thing after Dad pulled me out. I just didn't want to hear it back then." Luca shrugged. "Tomorrow you can watch me do it right. If there's even a current."

"There better be," Nico said, "or I'm pushing you in."

story:
Hunter sat on the low wall by the basketball courts, his right arm wrapped in a bright orange cast that everyone had already signed twice. Three weeks ago he had been racing Devon across the wet blacktop, slipped, and thrown his hands out in front of him the way anybody does. His left palm had skidded harmlessly. His right wrist had taken everything, and now the radius, the bone on the thumb side of his forearm, was knitting itself back together in a sleeve of fiberglass.

The doctor had told him something that kept circling back in his head. "Of all the broken bones we see in kids," she had said, scanning his x-ray, "a fracture of the radius near the wrist is the most common. Almost always from landing on an outstretched hand, like you did." Hunter had nodded then, but now he was watching the playground with new eyes, because Devon was about to test his theory.

"You're going to eat it on that patch," Hunter called. Devon was on his board, rolling toward the spot where the drainage grates made the pavement buckle. The new kid, Marcus, had an opaque monopoly on the good ramp by the fence, hogging it since lunch began, so everyone else had to make do with the broken ground.

"Watch me stick it," Devon said, and of course he didn't. The board shot sideways and Devon went down with both arms flung forward, palms slapping the blacktop. He bounced right up, shaking out his wrists, grinning.

"See?" Hunter said, hopping off the wall. "Everybody catches themselves the same way. Hands out. That's the pattern." He had started allocating his lunch periods to this, standing by the courts with a notebook, tallying every fall he witnessed. Twelve falls so far, twelve outstretched hands, four kids rubbing their wrists afterward. Two of them had ended up in the emergency room like him, one with a swollen wrist and a story identical to his own.

"So what do we do about it?" Devon asked. "Fall on our faces?"

"That's the problem," Hunter admitted. "You can't not put your hands out. It just happens." He looked down at his cast, at the signatures blurred where his thumb rubbed against it, and for the first time the orange didn't seem like a badge from a cool crash. It seemed like the tuition for a lesson he could never quite teach anyone, because the body never listens in the moment.

Devon picked up his board. "Race you to the wall," he said, and took off running.

Hunter ran after him, one-armed and slower, and lost.

Sebastian had been waiting for this watch party since Tuesday, and now that everyone was crowded into the living room, he could hardly sit still. Chips bowls covered the coffee table, his uncle had claimed the good armchair, and the pregame show blared while his cousins argued about which team would win. Only Grandpa Ray sat quietly near the window, polishing his glasses, and Sebastian noticed he was smiling like he knew a secret.

"You should have seen the very first one," Grandpa Ray announced during a commercial. "I remember it like yesterday. The Green Bay Packers beat the Kansas City Chiefs thirty-five to ten."

Sebastian frowned. Grandpa told great stories, but he also claimed he'd once shaken hands with a president, which nobody in the family believed. The first Super Bowl sounded ancient, older than Dad even. "Wait," Sebastian said, grabbing his tablet. "When was it?"

"January fifteenth, 1967," Grandpa said without hesitating.

Sebastian typed fast. The kickoff show returned on TV, everyone shouting, but he ignored it. If the date checked out, maybe the rest did too. His cousin Dana leaned over his shoulder. "What are you doing? You're missing the highlight reel!"

"Fact-checking Grandpa. He says he remembers the first Super Bowl."

Dana snorted. "Nobody remembers that. He probably made it up, like the president thing."

The search results loaded, and Sebastian froze. January 15, 1967. Green Bay Packers, Kansas City Chiefs, 35 to 10. Every number matched, exactly, with no wobble. He checked a second site, then a third, because a single page could be wrong. Dana kept tapping his arm, saying he should resign himself to the fact that Grandpa exaggerated, that the old man's stories were just an extravagant metaphor for a life he wished he'd lived. Sebastian shook her off.

"Grandpa," he said, standing up in front of the TV, which earned him a groan from his uncle. "It's all true. Every bit."

Grandpa Ray put on his glasses and grinned wider than Sebastian had ever seen. "Told you. And the president thing?" He paused dramatically. "That one's not true." The whole living room erupted, Dana laughing loudest, and she admitted she'd completely changed her mind about Grandpa's stories. She dropped onto the couch beside him and demanded he start from the beginning.

Just then the whistle blew, the game kicked off, and Grandpa leaned forward, pointing at the screen. "Now watch this next play. I've got a feeling about it."

story:
Austin slid into his chair just as his mom set down the spaghetti, and his phone buzzed against his leg before he even picked up his fork. It was the group chat. Someone had posted a screenshot of the photo he'd put on his page last night, the one of him asleep at his desk with his mouth open and a pencil stuck in his hair. He had deleted it after only ten minutes. Now here it was again, with a row of laughing emojis underneath.

"That's the third time your phone has buzzed since you sat down," his dad said, twirling noodles onto his fork. "Rule of the table, buddy."

"I know, I know." Austin put the phone face down, but his mind kept snagging on the problem like a sleeve on a nail. He had deleted the photo. He'd watched it disappear from his page himself. So how was it sitting in the chat, crisp and complete, as if it had never left? He took a bite and barely tasted it.

"Earth to Austin," his sister Maya said, waving a garlic bread stick at him. "The jury has decided you're being weird."

"The jury?" he said.

"Maya's class did a mock trial today," his mom explained, sprinkling parmesan. "She's very proud of her guilty verdict."

Austin pushed his plate forward a half inch, thinking. His sister would probably be the perfect person to ask, because she took screenshots constantly. "Maya, when you screenshot something, where does the picture actually go? Like, whose is it?"

She shrugged. "Mine. It's in my photos. It's just a copy I made." She bit the end off the bread stick. "Why? What did you post?"

Heat crawled up his neck. "Nothing. Hypothetically, if somebody deleted something from their page, could it still exist somewhere?"

"Sure," Maya said, like it was the most obvious thing in the world. "Deleting it takes it off your page. Anybody who already took a screenshot or saved a copy still has it."

story:
Jade sat in the exam room with her right arm propped on the paper-covered table, the fiberglass cast scratchy against her chin. Six weeks ago she had broken her radius falling off the garage roof while installing a birdhouse with her dad, and today, finally, the doctor would cut the cast off. In the waiting room she had seen a boy about her age leave with his arm out of a sling, and something about it had bothered her. His newly freed arm hung thinner than the other one, the skin pale, like a stick taped to his shoulder. She kept turning the image over in her mind, and by the time the nurse called her name, she had a guess: an arm that stays completely still for weeks loses something.

"So you think you can keep the muscles working from inside the cast?" her little brother Theo asked from the corner chair. He wanted her home by three, because he had plans for the two of them to build a model volcano before dinner, and every extra minute in this office felt like a stolen one.

"That's the idea," Jade said. "I've been squeezing this." She dug a stress ball out of her jacket pocket with her left hand, the one that had done everything for six weeks, and pressed it into her casted palm. Her fingers curled around it, faint and effortful, like they were moving through syrup. "Ten squeezes, four times a day, since week two. If stillness makes an arm shrink, then some movement should keep it from shrinking so much." She had no way to see inside the cast, which was the frustrating part. She could only measure the results today.

The saw whined, the shell split, and the two halves came away. Jade stared at her right arm and her stomach dropped. It was noticeably thinner than her left, the wrist narrow, the muscle of her forearm soft and small where the other one was round and firm. Her experiment had not saved it. "It's so skinny," she said, holding both arms side by side. "Why is it so much smaller?"

The doctor paused on his way out. "Muscles kept still in a cast weaken and shrink," he said. "That's normal." Then he was gone, and Jade turned back to her arm, flexing it, watching a small tremor run through it.

"Theo, grab my notebook," she said. She wanted to write this down while it was fresh: date, arm measurements, squeeze counts. Physical therapy would start next week, and the therapist had warned her that progress would hit a plateau at some point, where the arm would stop improving for a while no matter what she did. She intended to be ready with data, a whole coherent record from cast to recovery. Theo dug the notebook from her backpack and slapped it onto the table.

"Volcano at three," he said. "Deal?"

"Deal," Jade said, and wrote the first number down.

story:
George set the two bean pots side by side on the picnic table, then moved them apart again, because side by side meant the taller one would shade the shorter one, and he wasn't testing shade. His question was simpler: did the plant food he'd bought with three weeks of allowance actually make beans grow faster? Pot A got the food. Pot B got plain water. Everything else, he'd promised himself, would stay exactly the same.

For nine days it worked. Pot A pulled ahead, and George measured both stems every morning with a ruler he kept in his back pocket. Fourteen centimeters versus nine. He wrote the numbers in his lab notebook and tried not to grin, because a real scientist, he figured, would be more like an artisan with data, careful and unhurried, immune to showing off.

Then his little sister Nadia came outside with a popsicle and stopped by the table.

"Why is this one all leaning?"

George looked. Pot B, the plain-water pot, leaned hard toward the fence, its leaves angled sideways like they were trying to escape. Pot A stood straight. He walked around the table twice. Both pots had the same soil from the same bag, the same amount of water from the same cup, the same kind of seeds from the same packet. So why would one lean?

He got down on his knees and scrutinized the yard from pot level, the way a bug would see it. From there he could see it plainly: the picnic table sat half under the big maple, and Pot B was in the shade of the trunk for most of the afternoon, while Pot A caught the window-side sun. Sunlight came from one direction, so Pot B had been bending toward the bright strip along the fence.

He stood up fast. His whole experiment was broken. The fourteen-versus-nine comparison meant nothing, because the pots hadn't been treated the same. One sat in the sun and one didn't, so the difference in the plants could be sun or food or both mixed together, and he couldn't tell which. He pressed his palms flat on the table.

"What?" Nadia said, licking her popsicle.

"Everything was supposed to be the same except the food. That's the whole point. If anything else is different, I can't say the food did anything."

"So make them the same."

He moved both pots to the open middle of the yard, where neither one got shade and neither one leaned anywhere, and turned them so the leaves that had bent all faced the fence. Then he found a scrap of paper and wrote in his notebook: START OVER, DAY 1. FAIR TEST MEANS ONLY ONE THING CHANGES.

The science fair was in eleven days. Not much time, but enough, if nothing else moved. He poured the measured water into each pot, marked the levels with tape, and carried his ruler inside.

"Can I have the plant food for my Venus flytrap?" Nadia asked.

"No." He shut the screen door. "You'll confuse my variables."

"Wait, don't!" Autumn shot up from the table, arms out in front of her like a sleepwalker, bumping the doorframe before she found the hallway wall. She counted doorways in her head, the way she'd memorized them on a boring afternoon last summer, and felt her way into the kitchen. "We're not using candles. Where are the flashlights?"

Grandma paused with the matchbox in her hand. She looked at the candle stub, then at the flashlight, and set the matchbox back in the drawer. "I suppose the house has stood two hundred years. I'd like to preserve it a bit longer."

"So it's flashlights?" Autumn was already digging for the second one, the small one with the crank handle that her grandpa kept for camping trips.

"It's flashlights," Grandma agreed, and she laughed. "Look at me, changing my mind at my age."

They carried the lights out to the porch and sat on the swing, watching the stars come out over the dark valley, brighter than Autumn had ever seen them without the porch light washed out. The pizza got cold inside, but Autumn didn't care. She cranked the little flashlight and aimed its beam at the barn roof, then traced it along the fence line toward the road. Somewhere out there the power crews were working, and the lights would come back eventually, but for now the whole dark world belonged to them.

"Want to see how far the beam reaches?" Autumn asked, standing up on the porch rail.

If something invisible had gone wrong inside, he reasoned, the broken arm would fall behind the good one, week by week, and the numbers would disclose it before anyone could see it in a mirror.

"He told me once," Vincent said. "I'm checking."

"Hold that," he said. "I want it after."

Dex flipped it open. "Twenty-three, twenty-three, twenty-three. What is this, a math project?"

Their opponents were from Fairview, an affluent town with a fancy shaded dugout and matching coolers. Those kids looked fresh. Austin's whole team looked boiled. The air was already soaked, and it wouldn't take the sweat off his skin.

He grabbed the dugout's damp rag and hung it on the chain-link in the sun. Then he took the dry paper towels from the first aid kit and hung one beside it, after dunking it in his water bottle. The twist came after the game. Fairview's shortstop, the freshest kid on the field, collapsed in the handshake line, and Austin was the only one who wasn't surprised. He ran for the ice water first.

Adults average two to three colds a year, the pamphlet said, and children often catch even more than that. Ryder stood there holding the paper. Three colds in five months wasn't proof of anything broken. Three colds since fall was just... being twelve.

He heard footsteps and climbed back onto the table, keeping the pamphlet in his hand.

"So," Dr. Patel said, coming in with the folder open. "Third cold since fall, and you want to know if your immune system is broken. Here's the thing." He paused. "Actually, you go first. You've got a look on your face."

Ryder held up the pamphlet. "I already figured it out. Adults average two to three colds a year, and kids catch even more. So I'm basically normal." He hesitated. "I thought I was a walking science experiment."

Dr. Patel laughed. "I was going to tell you exactly that. You beat me to it."

"Mom's going to say I'm dramatic," Ryder said. "She has this whole anecdote about how I cried over a splinter when I was five, and she tells it every time I say anything hurts."

"Then here's your homework," Dr. Patel said, tearing a corner off the pamphlet and writing on it. "Show her this number. Three colds is right on schedule." He handed Ryder the scrap of paper, and Ryder folded it carefully and put it in his pocket with his library card, which was where he kept things that mattered.

"If I change the year," she said quietly, "nobody ever checks, right?" Sadie had been waiting for this Saturday for two weeks, and now that it was here, she was speeding past the pretzel stand at the mall like the optical shop might vanish if she slowed down. The optician, a woman with silver hoops and an eccentric purple vest covered in tiny glasses pins, laughed and pulled a tray from the back. "Let's find you something good." Sadie tried on pair after pair, and each one felt like a different version of herself, a movie star, a scientist, a mysterious spy. Finally she chose slim gray frames, and the whole shop seemed to radiate possibility while the optician slid the new lenses in.

That was when Priya walked in, waving. Priya was already a glasses veteran, and her ambition to become an optometter someday, her word for it, meant she knew all the shop's frames by name. "Ooh, those are so good on you," Priya said, then leaned close to the little mirror on the counter. "Wait. Look at us."

Sadie looked. Priya's lenses made her eyes look noticeably bigger, round and wide behind the glass. Sadie's own reflection showed the opposite: her eyes looked smaller. "Why would they do that?" Sadie asked. "We're both wearing glasses. Mine shrink my eyes and yours blow them up."

Priya shrugged, but Sadie couldn't let it go. She thought about it while the optician adjusted the fit behind her ears. If the lenses did opposite things to how their eyes looked, maybe the lenses themselves were opposite. She pulled her reading homework out of her backpack, held her new glasses up to the page, and read a line easily. Then she asked, "Priya, can I try yours?"

Priya handed them over, grinning like a lab partner. Sadie held Priya's glasses over her homework, and the words swam into blur. When Priya put Sadie's glasses on and tried to read her own magazine, she squinted and said, "Nope, everything close up is a mess."

"Because your lenses are the opposite of mine," Sadie said, snapping her fingers. "Yours make things look bigger. Mine make things look smaller." Priya's whole face lit up. "That's exactly it! The optician told me last year. My problem is farsightedness. The light in my eye focuses behind the retina, so stuff up close looks blurry, and convex lenses fix it." She tapped her frames. "Convex means they bulge out, so they magnify my eyes. Yours must be the opposite kind, because your eyes look smaller through them."

"So near stuff is blurry for me, far stuff is blurry for you," Sadie said, "and opposite lenses fix us." She put her glasses back on, picked up her homework, and read the first line out loud, fast and clear, savoring every crisp letter. Priya grabbed her arm and said, "Come on, we're testing them on the mall directory from way across the food court."

Eleanor stood at the edge of the festival lawn, where the food stalls gave way to a long table draped in blue cloth. Behind the table, a Torah scroll lay open on a wooden stand, its letters small and crowded, and a woman named Rabbi Ora was letting visitors look but not touch. Eleanor's bat mitzvah was in three weeks, and she still could not get through her portion without stumbling at the same verse. She had come here to petition the rabbi for extra practice, though she had rehearsed the asking all morning and now the words felt too big for her mouth.

"My reading keeps breaking in the same place," she finally said. "I thought maybe the scroll itself would help. Seeing it instead of the photocopy."

Rabbi Ora slid the scroll along the stand so the tricky verse faced Eleanor. "Read it here, out loud. The whole festival will hear you, so you might as well practice being nervous."

Eleanor began, and her voice wobbled exactly where it always did. She leaned closer, squinting at the tight rows of letters, and her finger drifted toward the parchment to hold her place.

"Use this instead." Rabbi Ora pressed a slim silver pointer into her hand, shaped like a small hand with one long finger. "It's called a yad."

"What does that mean?"

"Hand. The scroll doesn't get touched, so the reader follows the words with the yad instead of a finger."

Eleanor fit the silver finger beneath the line she was reading, and something unexpected happened. The verses she had been sure she hated, the ones she had grumbled about for a month, went smoothly, because she stopped losing her place. She had been biased against the whole passage, blaming the words themselves, when the real problem was that her eyes kept sliding off the line. Now the pointer held them still. She finished the verse, then the next one, and the crowd noise around the table seemed to fold itself away.

"That was it," she said, almost laughing. "That was the whole problem."

"It usually is," Rabbi Ora said. "Though you'll have to carry the melody alone at your ceremony. No excuses about photocopies then."

Eleanor looked down at the yad lying light in her palm, silver warming to her skin, and thought of the morning she would stand in front of everyone with this same scroll, her grandmother's congregation watching from the third row where her grandmother used to sit. She would get the words right now. That was the gain. The cost she understood only partly: some doors, once opened, showed you exactly how much you still owed.

She handed back the pointer and touched the silver one last time, right at the tip of its long finger.

The after-school Heritage Club met in the library on Tuesdays, and Kaitlyn had joined for one reason: she wanted a real answer about her own last name, Novak, which nobody at school could pronounce right. Today's ritual was the display table, where every member put out one object that stood for their family. She felt proud of the label until Dani, whose grandfather was Hungarian too, stopped in front of it and frowned.

"That's not a mistake," Dani said. He pulled a card out of his backpack, a birthday card his grandfather had signed for his mother: "Kovacs Peter" in careful blue ink. "My grandpa signs everything backwards like that. Mom says he does it on purpose."

Kaitlyn looked from the card to her postcard and felt something shift. If two people did the same thing, it probably was not a mistake at all. Maybe it was a pattern, and patterns meant a rule was hiding underneath it. She needed more evidence, so she went to find Min, who had brought a calligraphy scroll with her Korean name on it, "Kim Jiwoo," family name first, the way Min always wrote it. Kaitlyn set the card, the postcard, and the scroll side by side on the table.

"Dani's grandfather signs his family name first," she said slowly, testing the idea out loud. "My great-grandmother did the same thing. And your name is written that way too. Min, is that just a Korean thing, or could Hungarian work like that?"

"Korean, Japanese, Chinese, and Hungarian," Min said, pointing at the three objects in a row. "Same order in all of them. Family name first."

"So in Hungarian, a person's family name is written before the given name," Kaitlyn said, and as she said it, the whole table of objects rearranged itself in her mind. Her great-grandmother had not been confused. She had been following the custom of her own language, the same order used across the world in Chinese, Japanese and Korean names. Kaitlyn crossed out her label, and the smudge where "mistake" had been did not quite diminish her relief. It made it heavier, somehow.

"That's actually a legitimate reason to fix the sign," said Mr. Okafor from across the room, where he was stapling the banner for Friday's heritage night. Kaitlyn rewrote it: "Novak Anna, my great-grandmother, who wrote her name the Hungarian way." Then she sat back and looked at the corrected card, and a small ache settled in beside the satisfaction. She had solved the puzzle, but the woman who wrote that postcard was gone, and would never know that a great-granddaughter in a library had finally understood her.

"Friday night, you're reading this out loud," Dani said, tapping the postcard. "Both of us. Our grandfathers would like that."

Kaitlyn slid the postcard to the center of the table, next to Min's scroll, and left it there.

story:
Beatrice set the catapult on the kitchen table, loaded a marshmallow, and pulled the release arm. The marshmallow sailed across the room, bounced off the refrigerator, and landed in the fruit bowl.

"That's forty-two inches," said her little brother Oscar, holding the tape measure at arm's length like it might explode. "Can I have the marshmallow?"

"It touched the floor near the bowl. No." Beatrice wrote 42 on her data sheet under Trial 1, then frowned at it. Forty-two was great. Forty-two would probably win the science fair, or at least beat Dwight Yang's volcano, which had won for three years straight mostly because it glowed in the dark.

She reset the arm and launched again. This time the marshmallow went eleven inches and rolled off the table into Oscar's shoe.

"You wrote eleven," Oscar said, reading over her shoulder. "That's terrible. You should erase it and keep the forty-two."

Beatrice didn't erase it. Something about the two numbers bothered her. Same catapult, same marshmallow weight, same angle, and yet one throw went almost four times farther than the other. Either her machine was haunted, or one of those numbers was lying. She thought about the coin-flip unit from math class, how a single flip told you nothing but a hundred flips started showing something true. One launch might be a fluke. A fluke was exactly the kind of illusion that could win you a ribbon on Friday and embarrass you in front of the whole gym on Saturday, if the judges asked you to repeat it.

"I'm going to run it ten times," she announced.

"That's boring," said Oscar.

"Then count."

She launched, and launched, and adjusted the spoon cup a hair after trial six when it started rattling loose, and marked every distance down. The numbers wandered all over the place, 19, 33, 26, 15, 38, and none of them was 42 again, which made 42 look more and more like a freak. When she finished, she added all ten distances, divided by ten, and wrote the average at the bottom of the sheet: 27.4 inches.

"There," she said. "That's my real number."

"That's smaller than forty-two," Oscar pointed out. "You made your project worse on purpose."

"It's not worse, it's true. One lucky throw is just one lucky throw. If I run it ten times, the weird flukes kind of cancel out, and the average is what the catapult actually does." She tapped the 27.4. "That's the fundamental number. That one I can prove."

Oscar ate a marshmallow anyway when she wasn't looking, which she knew, because trial eleven had been sitting on the scale.

The next morning she brought the catapult to school in a shoebox. Dwight Yang was already in the hallway, plugging in his volcano. Beatrice looked at 27.4 on her data sheet, looked at the judges' table, and set up her first launch of the day.

Florence had typed and deleted her message to Marisol three times before her little brother Theo leaned over her shoulder. "You're doing the typing thing again," he said, flopping onto the couch with his tablet. She shooed him away, but gently, because Theo had spent all morning quiet and pale after his recital video had gone up on the school's music page and someone in the comments had called his solo "a crime scene." Florence's plan was to reply to that comment with something clever and cutting. The trouble was that every version she typed sounded either mean or desperate, and she couldn't tell which one it would be until after she posted it.

Instead of sending anything, she opened a new tab and looked up the school's music page itself. There was Theo, mid-note, under the headline "Winter Concert Highlights." An idea nudged her. If the video weren't public anymore, the comment couldn't keep stinging him every time someone Googled his name. The music teacher, Mr. Adeyemi, ran the page, but Florence knew from the contact line that he only checked email on Sundays. She noticed something else while she scrolled: a link at the bottom of the page, small and gray, to an archive site she'd heard kids mention, the Wayback Machine.

"Watch this," she told Theo, pulling him up by the sleeve. She pasted the music page's address into the archive's search box. A whole timeline appeared, row after row of dates going back years, like snapshots taken of the page while nobody was looking. "It says it's saved more than one trillion web pages," Theo read, his voice going up on the last word.

Florence clicked one of the older dates, and there was the page from two autumns ago, before Theo was even in band. It looked almost the same, except the photos showed kids who had graduated. She felt the idea settle into place, cold and clear. Even if the video came down tomorrow, an old copy might still be sitting in that trillion-page pile, waiting for anyone who went looking. Deleting something public didn't mean it vanished. It meant it vanished from one place.

"So my plan doesn't work," Theo said slowly.

"Your plan was to hide. My plan is different." She scrolled back to the current page and found the email link for Mr. Adeyemi. She drafted a message that didn't try to be clever, that didn't invade his inbox with drama, just said: the comments on the Winter Concert video are hurting my brother, and kids at school are sharing screenshots. Could the comment section be turned off? She read it aloud to Theo so he could hear how it sounded, because tone in an email was like tone in a voice, easy to get wrong without a face to check against.

He nodded, then pointed at her screen. "Add that he practices an hour a day. So Mr. Adeyemi knows the crime scene thing is a lie."

Florence typed the sentence in, and Theo, satisfied, went back to the couch and put his tablet face-down on the cushion, which he only did when he was done worrying about something. She hovered over the send button, then clicked it before she could start deleting again.

"Done," she said. "Now we wait until Sunday."

Juliette stood in front of the bathroom mirror with her chin tilted up, counting. Three on her forehead, one beside her nose, and a new one forming on her chin, red and tender. Last year her face had been clear, and this year it wasn't, and she wanted to know why.

At the pharmacy after school, she found the aisle with the face washes and started reading labels. "Oil-free," one said. "For acne-prone skin," said another. She turned a bottle over and squinted at the back. It mentioned unclogging pores. Pores, oil, pimples. Those three words kept coinciding on every label, and she didn't think that was an accident.

Her little brother Marcus appeared beside her, eyeing the candy shelf across the aisle. "Why are you reading shampoo for ten minutes?"

"It's not shampoo." She held up the bottle. "It says it fights pimples by unclogging pores. So pores get clogged with something."

"With dirt," Marcus said.

"Maybe. Or oil." She set the bottle down and picked up another, a scrub with the word "vigorous" splashed across the front, promising a deep clean. On the back, in smaller letters, it mentioned excess oil. She thought about her own face, shiny by lunch even when she washed it in the morning, and about her cousin Leo, who was eleven and whose face was never shiny at all. The difference was that Leo was younger. Something about getting older had changed her skin, and whatever it was, it was making more oil.

"Marcus, if I washed my face five times a day, would that fix it?"

He shrugged. "You'd be very clean."

She felt some skepticism about that plan herself. Washing had never stopped the shine before, so plain dirt didn't seem like the whole story. She took out her phone and typed carefully: why do teenagers get pimples. She scrolled, then stopped at a line that made everything click into place. Puberty hormones made the oil glands in her skin produce more oil, and the extra oil could clog pores, which led to acne.

"It's oil," she said. "There's even a word for it. Sebum."

"Sounds like a potion ingredient."

"It's the stuff clogging my pores." She put the vigorous scrub back, because scrubbing harder wouldn't change how much oil her glands made, and chose instead a gentle wash marked "non-comedogenic," which the label explained meant it wouldn't clog pores. Two weeks, the bottle suggested, before anyone should expect results. That felt long, but at least now she had a real reason for what was happening instead of just blaming herself for being careless.

At home, she set the new bottle on the sink where she would actually see it, morning and night. Her chin still had the tender spot, and her forehead still had its three, but she uncapped the wash, wet her hands, and started anyway. "Twenty-eight washes till the verdict," she told the mirror. "I can wait."

His right arm hung in a cast that itched in the afternoons, and under his jacket he had hidden something folded twice: the X-ray film from his wrist, taken three weeks ago at the clinic. Jeremy unfolded the film and held it up against the low sun. "Look at this. The bones glow like they're lit from inside. My skin's barely there, just a gray smudge. Why does the picture work like that?"

Marisol took the film and tilted it. "Because of the calcium. Bones show up white on an X-ray because the calcium in them absorbs more X-rays than the softer tissue around them. The soft stuff lets the rays pass through, so it hardly shows at all."

Jeremy sat down beside her and studied the white bones again, the two broken edges of his radius angled toward each other like friends about to shake hands. "So the dark gap between them," he said slowly, "that's where the rays went straight through. That's the break."

"Right. No calcium bridge yet, so no white." She pointed to a faint haze already forming at the edges of the gap. "But see that? That's new bone starting to fill in."

Jeremy's dilemma had been simple all week: the coach wanted him at practice throwing left-handed, and Jeremy wanted to sit out entirely until the arm was whole. Now he traced the haze with his finger, thinking. If white meant calcium, and calcium meant bone, then the way to know whether he was healing was to see whether that gap kept getting whiter. He couldn't watch it, not without another X-ray, but he could test the idea a different way. "They took two pictures," he said, pulling the older film from his jacket, the one from the day of the break. He laid them side by side on the metal bench. In the first, the gap yawned wide and black. In the second, it had narrowed, and the haze of white crept further along both broken edges.

"It's working," Jeremy said. "It's actually closing." He looked up, and the first cold drops of rain dotted the films, so they gathered them quickly and ran for the equipment shed, Jeremy holding both X-rays flat against his chest with his good hand, Marisol laughing and pulling her hood up as they ran.

story:
Ryder spent twenty minutes deciding between his conventional blue shirt and the green one nobody had ever seen him wear. He picked green, then changed his mind, then changed it back. His little sister, Nadia, watched from the doorway with a bowl of cereal. "I nominate the green one," she said. "You look like somebody who's about to do something interesting." Ryder frowned at the mirror. "It's just a dance, Nadia." But he kept the green shirt on.

The gym smelled like floor wax and punch, and the music hit him before he even got through the doors. Marcus was waiting near the refreshment table, waving him over. "You came! Okay, the eighth graders are on that side, the seventh graders claim the far wall, and Priya said she might dance with anybody who asks nicely. That's the factor that decides your whole night, basically." Ryder laughed, but his palms were sweating, and not only about Priya.

They drifted toward the stage, where two speakers taller than Mr. Hobbes stood on either side of the DJ booth. The bass thumped in Ryder's chest like a second heartbeat. After one song, his ears felt strange, a tight, fuzzy pressure, and he noticed Marcus rubbing his ear with the heel of his hand. "Yours too?" Ryder asked. Marcus nodded. "It's like they're full of static."

Ryder's phone had an app he'd opened once for a science homework option, a sound meter. He pulled it out and held it up. The number on the screen wobbled around 88 near the speakers. He remembered the chart from that same homework, the one about safe listening: exposure to 85 decibels was okay for eight hours a day, but each 3-decibel increase cut that safe time in half. So 88 wasn't just a little more than 85. It was half the safe time, four hours. And if the meter was reading low, if they were really at 91, that would be two hours. They had been standing there for maybe twenty minutes, and his ears already felt like static. "Let's test something," Ryder said. "We walk toward the far wall and check the number."

They walked. Ten steps, the number dropped to 85. Ten more, and it hovered at 82. By the seventh grade wall, it read 79, and the pressure in Ryder's ears loosened like a fist unclenching. "Whoa," Marcus said, staring at the screen. "So three points is half? That's wild. My brother stands by those speakers all night." Ryder pocketed the phone. "Not me. I plan to hear things when I'm eighty." Marcus grinned. "You're the most careful reckless person I know."

Priya appeared beside them with two cups of punch, holding one out. "You two look like scientists at a concert. What are you studying?" Ryder took the cup, and the fuzzy feeling in his ears was almost gone. "Acoustics," he said. "Want me to tell you about it?" She sipped her punch and shrugged. "Only if you tell me while we dance." Ryder set his cup down on the table and held out his hand.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
story:
The car smelled like grandma's house anyway, because the paper lantern Logan held in his lap had been hers, folded flat and tucked in her dresser for years. Outside, huge white wind turbines turned slowly above the hills, each blade sweeping past like a slow hand waving. Dad had the gearshift in neutral at the long red light, his face set and careful, and Mom kept her eyes on the map even though she already knew the way.

"You're sure it's tonight?" Dad asked.

"That's the whole point," Logan said. "It's mid-August. Obon is mid-August. That's when her spirit comes home for a visit, so if we're going to put the lantern out at her house, tonight is when it counts." He had worked this out over three days, checking the calendar twice, deciding he had to prioritize this over the soccer camp he'd already paid for. Coach Ray had not been happy. That was the cost, and Logan had agreed to pay it.

At Grandma's dark house, Dad unlocked the front door and Logan went straight for the kitchen drawer where she kept her old datebooks. He wanted proof, some sign she had done this herself. The summer before she died, in her careful handwriting, was one word: Obon. But it was written in July, not August, and in the datebook from the year before, July again.

"July," he said out loud, feeling the floor tilt under the plan he'd built. "Most places do it in mid-August, but her hometown was one of the places that did it in July. All along, I was a month off. I missed it. I missed it for this year."

Mom crouched beside him. "You didn't miss her," she said. "You just missed the date."

So the lantern went up anyway. Logan unfolded it on the porch steps, and Dad lit the small candle inside, cupping the flame against the breeze coming off the hills. The paper glowed warm orange, and somewhere down the valley one of the turbines caught the last sunlight and flashed. It was the wrong week, maybe even the wrong month, and the house behind them was empty and would be sold by fall.

"Want to say something?" Dad asked.

Logan thought about it, then shook his head. "She'd rather hear the game anyway." So he sat on the steps and told the lantern, quietly, how the team had done without him this week, and how he'd kind of ruined a penalty kick, and how she would have laughed.

The candle fluttered, then steadied.

story:
Eleanor had five dollars and one goal: the box of old comic books on the far table. She had circled the garage sale twice already, pretending to look at lampshades, because the man next to her kept pulling comics out one at a time and reading them. When he finally wandered off toward the record crates, she darted in and grabbed the box, only to hear the seller say, "Those are three dollars each now."

"Each?" Eleanor said. "The sign says a dollar."

The seller shrugged and flipped the cardboard sign over, where a new price was written in fresh marker. "That was before four people asked about them in the last half hour. Only two full boxes left. Somebody just offered to buy a whole box." His prices were volatile, changing whenever the crowd around a table thickened or thinned, and Eleanor had watched a stack of encyclopedias drop from ten dollars to two when nobody touched it for an hour.

She was still holding the box when she noticed a thin old book at the bottom, wedged under the comics. The cover was cracked leather, and inside, in faded ink, someone had copied a passage. It began: "Nothing is more useful than water, yet it will buy scarcely anything, while a diamond can buy a great deal." Eleanor read it twice. She carried the book to the seller. "What is this?"

"'The Wealth of Nations'," he said. "Published in 1776. My grandfather acquired it at an estate sale, and it's the one thing here I'm not discounting."

Eleanor looked at the sentence again. Water was the most useful thing there was, and it cost almost nothing, while a tiny diamond could buy piles of stuff. She looked at the tables around her: the comics, scarce and fought over, climbing in price; a whole driveway of drinking glasses, dozens of them, marked down to a quarter. She thought of the treaty of comic collectors who had apparently agreed, without ever meeting, that these particular issues mattered. Something invisible was setting every price on this lawn, something she couldn't see but could almost touch now.

"I'll give you my five dollars for this book and two comics," she said, holding her breath.

The seller studied her, then the thinning crowd, and said, "Four dollars, because it's almost noon and you're the only one who asked about that book all morning."

Eleanor counted out the bills, tucked the book under her arm, and walked home reading as she went.

story:
Olivia had been postponing the question all afternoon, but at three o'clock it caught up with her: what do you bring to dinner at a house where you don't know the rules? Her new friend Nadia had invited her over for her birthday, and Nadia's family had moved to town from Malaysia only two months ago. Olivia's own family was eccentric enough that her grandmother kissed strangers on both cheeks and refused to let anyone start eating before a toast, so she knew that every household ran on its own invisible rules. She just couldn't see these ones yet.

She brought a small box of chocolates, wrapped hastily in gold paper, and stood on the porch rehearsing a greeting. When Nadia's father opened the door, he smiled and offered his right hand. Olivia shook it and passed him the gift, also with her right hand, mostly because that was the hand she used for everything. He accepted it the same way, thanked her warmly, and said, "In Malaysia, where we come from, we give and receive with the right hand, as a sign of respect."

In the dining room, Olivia noticed a pattern. Every dish was passed right hand to right hand, and when Nadia's little brother reached across the table with his left, Nadia caught his wrist and switched it for him without a word. Olivia filed that away and watched harder. Nobody said anything about it. The rule was quiet, like her grandmother's toast.

Then the rice arrived, and Olivia realized she had been holding her fork in her left hand all evening, the way her uncle had taught her, scooping with the spoon on the right. Her stomach dropped. Had she been rude for the last twenty minutes without knowing? She considered the probability that no one had noticed and decided it was low, because Nadia's grandmother kept glancing at her plate. Olivia had a simple idea: she would test it. She set the fork down, picked up the spoon with her right hand alone, and took the next bite.

Nadia's grandmother smiled at her, a real smile with crinkled eyes, and pushed the chicken dish toward her side of the table. Olivia reached out with her right hand and served herself. Across the table, Nadia gave her a tiny nod.

After dinner, Nadia pulled her into the kitchen and whispered, "Grandma says you have good manners. She wants to know if you'll come for Hari Raya in the spring."

"Only if you come to my grandmother's house first," Olivia said. "She has rules too. There's a toast, and there's a zero percent chance of escaping it."

"Deal," said Nadia, and handed her the last chocolate from the box, with her right hand.

story:
Nathaniel spread the wires across the kitchen table and counted them twice. Copper, nichrome, and the steel paperclip he had straightened that morning, each one meant to carry current to the same small bulb. The science fair was Thursday, and his data sheet was a mess.

He clipped the copper wire to the battery holder, and the bulb glowed a steady yellow. He wrote down "bright." Then he swapped in the steel wire and a different bulb, because the first one had rolled off the table and he could not find it. The new bulb glowed pale and dim. He wrote "dim" and stared at it. Steel should have been worse than copper, but was the dimness the wire, or the other bulb? He had no way to know. He slammed the notebook shut, and his little sister Maya looked up from her cereal.

"You broke it already?"

"No. I don't know what I measured." He unrolled the crumpled handout from his back pocket and smoothed it flat. Maya leaned over her bowl and read the top line out loud. "Independent variable, the one thing you change on purpose. Dependent variable, what you measure to see the effect."

Nathaniel read it again, lips moving. He had changed two things. The wire and the bulb. That was the problem, sitting there in his own handwriting. "I changed the wire on purpose," he said slowly, "but I also changed the bulb by accident. So the brightness doesn't tell me anything about the wire."

"That's what you get for using my bulbs without asking."

He ignored her. The heater had been running all morning and the air in the kitchen felt arid enough to make the tape crackle when he peeled it off the table, but he kept working. He needed one bulb, the same bulb, every single trial. He searched under the table, found the runaway bulb in the shadow of the chair leg, and taped it down so it could not escape again. Copper went in. Bright. Steel went in, same bulb, same battery. The glow weakened to a dull orange, and this time the difference had to be the wire, because nothing else had moved.

For the last test he used the knife to strip the insulation and expose an inch of the copper, then the steel, then the nichrome, laying the bare metal in a neat row so the clips would touch clean conductor every time. Same battery. Same bulb. Three trials, three honest numbers. Maya slid her empty bowl toward him.

"You still owe me a bulb."
